question: How does a linked list work, and how does it compare to an array?

scenes.sub: Nodes chained by pointers: cheap to insert, slow to reach.
scenes.say: A linked list is the simplest structure built from pointers, and interviewers love it. Let's see how it works, and when it beats an array.

scenes.head: A treasure hunt
scenes.say: Imagine a treasure hunt. You hold a start card that says where the first clue is. Each clue holds a prize, and tells you where the next clue is. The last clue says: nowhere, you are done. To reach clue three, you must follow every clue before it. That is a linked list. The start card is the head, each clue is a node, and each where is a pointer.

scenes.head: A node, and three pointer moves
scenes.say: A node is a value plus a pointer to the next node. Insert at the head: make a node, point it at the old first, then move head to it. Insert after a node you hold: same two steps in the middle. Erase after: remember the doomed node, skip over it, then delete it. Nothing shifts. Each move is just a few pointer changes.

scenes.head: Insert 5 at the head

arrows.cue: move head to the new node

changes.cue: move head to the new node
move head to the new node

changes.text: wrong order: head moved first, 10 20 30 lost

scenes.say: Start with ten, twenty, thirty. Head points at ten. Insert five at the head. First, make the new node. Second, point it at ten, the old first. Third, move head to the new node. Order matters. If you move head first, you lose the rest of the list, because nothing points at ten anymore. Insert at the head costs O of one.

scenes.head: Delete 20 from the middle

changes.cue: Walk to the node before it
Walk to the node before it

scenes.say: Now delete twenty. Walk to the node before it, ten. Call that p. Step one: remember the doomed node, twenty. Step two: point ten past it, straight at thirty. Twenty is now cut out of the chain. Step three: delete it, or the memory leaks. Finding the previous node costs O of n, but the unlinking itself is O of one.

scenes.head: List versus array
scenes.say: Compare with an array. Reading item five is instant in an array, but a list must walk. Inserting at the front: an array shifts everything, a list changes two pointers. Insert or delete next to a node you already hold: constant time for a list. But arrays sit in one block of memory, so the cache loves them, while list nodes are scattered, and each carries a pointer. In practice, vector wins most of the time.

scenes.head: In the interview
rows: Why not always use a list?
No index access, poor cache behavior, extra memory. A vector is usually faster.
Doubly has a prev pointer too, so you can unlink a node without finding its predecessor.
Does C plus plus have one?
Yes. std::list is doubly linked, std::forward_list is singly linked.
Moving head before saving the old first node, or forgetting the empty list.
scenes.say: Follow-ups. Why not always use a list? No index access, and poor cache behavior. Singly or doubly linked? Doubly has a prev pointer, so unlinking is easy. Does C plus plus have one? Yes, s t d colon colon list is doubly linked. Classics: Delete Node in a Linked List, Remove Nth Node From End. The common mistake: moving head before saving the old first node.

lines: A node holds a value and a pointer to the next node.
Insert or delete is O(1) once you hold the node: just re-point, in the right order.
Reaching item k is O(n), so a vector usually wins.
